title: Require expand/contract sequencing for destructive schema migrations

approvals.evidence: "Write a policy doc (Recommended)" -- selected via AskUserQuestion, 2026-09-06, in response to the assistant naming this as one of two remaining review items needing explicit direction.

body.context: The 2026-09-06 industry-standard review's Prisma/Postgres conventions dimension raised a HIGH finding: nothing in this repository's process states that a destructive migration (drop/rename a column, narrow a type) must ship no earlier than the application code that stops needing the old shape. Migration 20260826000002_rich_content_json backfilled Issue.description/IssueNote.body into a new JSON shape and dropped the originals in the same migration, deployed to production while the application was still reading/writing the old plain-text shape -- the deployed Overview tab threw rendering a JSON object as a React child, and the intake mailbox watcher wrote plain strings into the new column as bare JSON string values. Reverted within the hour (20260826000003_revert_rich_content_json) and correctly redone the next day in the same deploy as the reading code (20260827000001_rich_content_json).
body.decision: Any migration that would break an existing reader or writer of the current schema shape is split into two migrations: an expand step (add the new shape, backfill it, ship whenever convenient) and a contract step (drop the old shape, ships no earlier than the same deploy as the application code that has fully stopped using it). A single migration may do both only when nothing currently deployed reads or writes what is being removed.

alternatives.option: A migration linter or CI check enforcing this mechanically
alternatives.rejected_because: Worth doing later, but needs a machine-readable notion of "currently deployed" this repository does not yet track; recording the rule in writing does not block adding enforcement afterward.

alternatives.option: Leave it as the unwritten convention the redo migration already followed
alternatives.rejected_because: The redo migration's own comment states the rule in prose, but a rule stated once inside one migration's comment is not discoverable by the next person writing a migration.

alternatives.option: Rewrite the historical migrations to look like they always followed this pattern
alternatives.rejected_because: The revert-then-redo sequence is the evidence this decision cites; editing it away removes the one concrete illustration of the failure mode.

consequences: A destructive schema change now costs two migrations and two deploys where it might have been one -- deliberately, for the class of change that broke production the one time this wasn't followed
Purely additive migrations (new column, new table, new index) are unaffected and still ship whenever ready
The historical migrations cited stay exactly as they are; this rule governs migrations written from here forward
